chunks.text: Dataset Initial Dataset A total of 541 images were used to prepare the datasets, with 410 allocated to training and validation along with 131 allocated to testing. The training images include the following: • 181 are digital photographs of elephant ivory tusks and carved ivory. 85 of these were provided by the School of Law in the University of Portsmouth as a part of the University of Portsmouth Ivory Project collection. These particular images have a resolution of 4928 × \times 3264 pixels. In addition, 96 of the images were newly photographed using a Canon PowerShot SX540 HS camera. These images have a resolution of 5184 × \times 3456 pixels. All of the mentioned images are in JPG format. • 106 are digital photographs of items resembling carved ivory. These objects are made from bone, horn or plastic and can be legally sold. Of these, 31 images were provided by the School of Law of the University of Portsmouth, 75 were new images photographed using a Canon PowerShot SX540 HS camera. The resolution of the mentioned images is 5184 × \times 3456 pixels. The images are in the JPG format. • A total of 123 images were obtained from Wikimedia Commons [ 27 ] under a public domain license. These comprise 41 images of ivory and 82 images of bone objects. The images are provided in a range of file formats and resolutions. The used images contain a wide selection of objects ranging from tusks to ivory and bone tools, jewellery, animal and human figurines and other museum exhibits. Some of the ivory objects show clearly visible Schreger lines while others do not. Objects are of different sizes and the photographs were taken under different lighting conditions with different color backgrounds (see Figs 1 , 6 and 7 ). This factor, in particular, makes it more difficult to train our algorithm; however, the diversity of the images makes our dataset more realistic and more akin to the images displayed in online marketplaces.

While this diversity supports our proof-of-concept approach, we acknowledge important differences between our dataset and real marketplace listings. Our images predominantly comprise of professionally photographed specimens, whereas sellers often use poor lighting, non-standard framing, and obfuscation tactics. The dataset size (541 images) reflects a practical constraint: we exhausted all publicly available ivory and bone images in Wikimedia Commons with appropriate licensing, supplemented by institutional and newly photographed specimens. The heterogeneous sources and class imbalance may introduce subtle biases, but the dataset is appropriate for transfer learning-based proof-of-concept work. Operational deployment will require substantially larger datasets (10,000+ images) from marketplace sources, including images with poor lighting conditions and photographs used for deliberate misrepresentation. Image Augmentation Note that the numbers listed above (i.e., 410 images used for training) refer only to the number of original images in the dataset and do not include those generated through image augmentation. Image augmentation refers to the technique of increasing the dataset size by applying various transformations to the images, such as cropping, rotating, reflecting, and resizing. In our case, we applied a number of different augmentation strategies. In particular, in order to explore the effectiviness of different augmentation methods, we generated four distinct versions of the original training dataset, which were then used to train four distinct machine learning models. These models were as follows: • Model I: No augmentation. Each image is resized to 400 × 400 400\times 400 pixels.

• Model II: Images are resized to 400 × 400 400\times 400 pixels and subjected to a standard augmentation pipeline provided by the fastai library [ 12 ] : random horizontal flips; rotations drawn uniformly from [ − 10 ∘ , + 10 ∘ ] [-10^{\circ},+10^{\circ}] ; zoom factors drawn uniformly from [ 1.0 , 1.1 ] [1.0,1.1] ; random perspective warping with a maximum warp coefficient of 0.2 0.2 ; and random brightness/contrast adjustments with a maximum lighting change of 0.2 0.2 . The affine and lighting transforms are each applied independently with probability 0.75 0.75 . • Model III: same as Model II, but Resize is replaced by RandomResizedCrop : a rectangular region is sampled uniformly such that it covers at least 30 % 30\% of the original image area and with a random aspect ratio, and is then resized to 400 × 400 400\times 400 pixels. This forces the network to be invariant to both scale and spatial location of the subject within the frame. • Model IV: same as Model III, with two additional colour augmentation strategies applied on top of the standard pipeline: random hue shifts drawn uniformly from [ − 0.25 , + 0.25 ] [-0.25,+0.25] (on a scale where 1.0 1.0 corresponds to a full 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} rotation of the colour wheel, i.e. up to ± 90 ∘ \pm 90^{\circ} ), and random saturation adjustments with a maximum factor of 0.5 0.5 . These colour augmentations are intended to make the classifier robust to variations in photographic lighting conditions and camera colour balance. With the listed augmentation methods applied to a random subset of images during each epoch of the training procedure, the effective number of images seen by the algorithm is then in the range of 2500–3000 images given the settings we used for training (see the Model subsection).

Note that the range of obtained images corresponds to the stochastic nature of the listed augmentation procedures resulting in a different number of total images, depending on which particular data samples were chosen to be in the training dataset. Method Ivory-bone object classification requires two separate steps: to identify the location of the item in the image, and then to classify the object as ivory or not ivory. This approach needs to be generalised in case multiple objects are present in the image. In computer vision, this problem can be addressed with a semantic image segmentation approach (e.g., see [ 16 ] for an overview). Semantic segmentation is the process of assigning for each pixel in an image the class to which it belongs; hence it is equivalent to a classification problem per pixel. Fig 1 shows an example of semantic segmentation for 2 pictures from our dataset. From the lower images we notice that this approach does not distinguish instances of the same class, i.e. two objects which belong to the same category will be labelled in the same way. Fig 1: Example of semantic segmentation.

The original images are shown on the left, while the images on the right show the classification targets. Red pixels correspond to the ivory class, green pixels to non-ivory, and black pixels to the background (images from Wikimedia Commons under the public domain license). The benefit of semantic segmentation is that it does not explicitly require identifying the location of the object in the image. On the downside, training an image segmentation model is time-consuming because it requires manually labeling the available images. For each image in our dataset, we created a “mask” similar to the one shown in Fig 1 using the graphical image annotation tool labelme 3 3 3 https://github.com/wkentaro/labelme . [ 25 ] . Finally, each pixel of each image was then classified as “ivory”, “non-ivory” or “background” using the U-net based approach described in the Model subsection. Our choice of transfer learning and semantic segmentation was informed by the dataset limitations outlined above. Transfer learning leverages pre-trained features from ImageNet [ 7 ] , mitigating the impact of our relatively small training set and heterogeneous image sources by reducing the effective domain shift between museum-quality images and marketplace listings. Semantic segmentation at the pixel level allows the model to identify discriminative features (e.g., Schreger lines) regardless of image quality or background variation, providing robustness across source heterogeneity. However, the class imbalance in our training data (roughly 63% ivory, 37% bone) may bias predictions toward the majority class. To account for this, we employ a threshold-based classification scheme (see section Results) that allows the model to express uncertainty, providing a more nuanced assessment than hard binary classification. Model We create a framework for semantic segmentation using the U-net model [ 21 ] with Resnet34 architecture [ 9 ] as backbone.

Fig 2 shows our architecture, which is similar to the first U-net originally developed for biomedical image segmentation [ 21 ] . This particular model was chosen due to its proven track record with small datasets (e.g. 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1,000 ) \mathcal{O}(1,000) images). To improve the performance and to reduce the training time the first half of the U-net (encoder) was initialised using weights pre-trained over the ImageNet 4 4 4 https://www.image-net.org/ . dataset. This approach is called “Transfer Learning” [ 30 ] and it generally helps with saving on computational, financial and environmental costs related to the training procedure. Fig 2: The U-Net architecture used for image segmentation. The U-net architecture consists of a contracting path (left side) made of down-sampling units, followed by an expansive path (right side) consisting of up-sampling units. Each down-sampling unit consists of convolution layers that extract features from the input images, and a max-pooling layer to reduce the size of the feature map. The extracted features are passed down to the next down-sampling unit and the corresponding up-sampling unit. We develop our model using fastai and its DynamicUnet class [ 12 ] . fastai is a high-level API on top of PyTorch [ 18 ] . The DynamicUnet class automatically creates a model adapting the intermediate feature sizes in accordance with the image size. We trained the U-Net using only the ivory and bone images, after splitting the dataset into 80% for training and 20% for validation. We trained the model for 20 epochs using Google Colaboratory 5 5 5 https://colab.research.google.com/ . , which is a cloud-based Jupyter notebook environment that lets users execute code directly through a web browser with access to free GPU and TPU compute resources. The number of training epochs was determined by trial and error – we found 20 epochs to be sufficient for the model to converge in all considered cases.

Using various image resizing and augmentation strategies we reach accuracies ranging between 90% and 95% on the training dataset, where the accuracy is defined as the average fraction (arithmetic mean) of pixels, which do not belong to the background and that are well classified. Results We tested our model using a set of 131 unseen images, taken from the publicly available archive at Wikimedia Commons [ 27 ] . This set consists of 73 images of carved ivory and 58 images of bone objects, photographed using different setups and under different lighting conditions. As before, the number of images was increased to around 800 via image augmentation. The photography information was generally not provided by the owner (e.g., metadata; however, note that metadata is not used in any way in our approach). The identification labels of each image (ivory or bone) were double-checked by an expert in elephant ivory identification, and only the confirmed images were used in the final dataset. Fig 3 shows the receiving operating characteristic (ROC) curve for the ivory classifier. The ROC curve evaluates the performance of the classifier for each classification threshold, i.e.

choosing different p ^ \hat{p} values to distinguish ivory carvings from bone. In particular, the area under the ROC curve (AUC) presents an aggregate measure of the classifier performance and can be interpreted as the probability that the model ranks ivory more highly than bone. In addition, we report other statistics of interest, including precision, recall, F1-score, area under the curve (AUC) and the Youden’s J statistic. The mentioned statistics are provided for the full test dataset in Table 1 . In Table 2 , we provide the listed statistics for the test predictions that are categorized as confident . This is defined as predictions for which the averaged ivory probability excess is higher than a chosen threshold value, i.e., | p ^ | > 0.3 |\hat{p}|>0.3 . We find that the best-performing model’s AUC value is 0.81 for the full dataset and 0.86 for the confident predictions dataset. We also provide the confusion matrices for the full test dataset and the confident predictions in Fig. 4 and 5 correspondingly. Fig 3: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for the ivory classifier. The area under the ROC curve is 0.81. The model performs significantly better than a random classifier (shown by the dashed line). Figs 6 and 7 show the predictions for a sample of carved ivory and bone images from the test set. The colorbar values are related to the probability assigned to each pixel of belonging to each class (i.e. ivory, bone, or background). Specifically, a lighter color indicates that a given pixel is more likely to be identified as ivory, while darker colors refer to the bone class. Similarly, white pixels are assigned to the background class. Note that the model accurately identifies the targeted objects in all images, even when multiple items are present. The background is correctly segmented, even when it is non-uniform, as illustrated in the first example of Fig 6 .

As before, images with | p ^ | < 0.3 |\hat{p}|<0.3 are classified as “uncertain”, indicating that the model cannot clearly determine the material of the item. Setting these thresholds, the model predicts the correct class for 59% of the images, the wrong class for 14%, and is uncertain for the remaining 27% of the cases. For test images on which the algorithm is confident (for the best scoring model), this corresponds to an overall classification accuracy of 83%. The threshold values for p ^ \hat{p} were determined experimentally; it is therefore possible that improved results could be achieved through hyperparameter tuning, which we leave for future work. In general, the algorithm gives mostly accurate predictions for the items that clearly show evidence of Schreger lines (e.g. the bottom image in Fig 6 ). However, as shown in the third example of Fig 6 , the model tends to miscategorize objects which have bright spots, even if they present Schreger lines. Note that even if the color of the objects does not seem to affect the classification results significantly, we notice a strong correlation between the prediction class and the lighting conditions in the image. The model has a tendency to classify darker objects as ivory, while well-lit pictures are often predicted to contain bone items. The accuracy figures listed above are best interpreted in the context of human performance. For example, a classification accuracy of 81% represents strong performance when compared to an ivory expert working without access to the objects themselves, relying solely on limited-resolution images and no additional information. A valuable direction for future work would be to have an independent ivory expert classify the test images in our dataset, providing an important benchmark against which to compare our results.

Discussion In this work, we have presented one of the first attempts to use computer vision techniques to identify ivory items solely from pictures (other similar approaches include [ 10 , 29 ] ). Our goal is to develop a tool that could help law enforcement officers to identify illegal trading of ivory in online marketplaces. The task is extremely challenging due to the great variety of ivory carvings and the presence of materials that resemble ivory. Moreover, being a biological material, ivory tends to change in color with age and exposure to light. We addressed the problem using a semantic image segmentation approach and we focused on distinguishing ivory carvings from bone items. Our model shows a good predictive ability when evidence of the type of material (e.g. Schreger lines) is visible. However, we identify a clear dependence of the classification accuracy on the lighting of the item in the image. The statistical analysis performed on the test dataset (Tables 1 and 2 ) also provides valuable insight into promising image augmentation strategies. First, the primary challenge to our approach is the small size of the training dataset. This is illustrated by the underperformance of Model I in Tables 1 and 2 . Second, different augmentation strategies significantly improve almost all of the considered statistics; however, the type of augmentation strategy employed matters. In particular, the best-scoring model, Model III, implements a wide range of augmentation transformations, including random rotations, zooms, warping transformations, brightness and contrast adjustments, and random crops. However, when random hue and saturation transformations are added to this set (Model IV), the algorithm predicts ivory in most cases. This provides another valuable indication that lighting conditions and colour scheme are among the key features that the algorithm uses to distinguish ivory from bone.

Overall, these results reaffirm the importance of training dataset size and image diversity. The issues identified here could be further mitigated by obtaining a larger dataset, as well as by employing generative AI methods to perform additional image augmentation. It is also important to discuss our results in a wider context of different detection and classification of ivory techniques. Traditional approaches to ivory identification rely on destructive or access-dependent methods. Microscopy, for instance, identifies ivory through diagnostic morphological features—most notably Schreger lines, but requires direct physical access to specimens and expert interpretation. Spectroscopy-based approaches (primarily Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy) provide definitive chemical identification and are non-destructive, yet similarly demand in-person specimen analysis and specialized laboratory infrastructure. By contrast, our computer vision approach operates solely on photograph evidence, enabling rapid screening of online marketplace listings where physical access is impractical. However, this strength comes with limitations: our study focuses on distinguishing processed ivory carvings from bone objects in relatively high-quality images. Real-world marketplace listings often feature poor lighting, obstructed views, and deliberate misrepresentation that may degrade performance compared to laboratory-quality specimens. Additionally, our current model cannot differentiate between freshly carved ivory and aged historical pieces, or identify ivory from specific elephant populations—capabilities achievable with spectroscopic methods. These limitations underscore that image-based AI classification is best positioned as a complementary first-pass screening tool rather than a definitive replacement for traditional forensic methods.

Despite the challenges, our model demonstrates solid predictive ability (for such a small dataset size), with potential for further improvement through enhanced tuning. We are now in a position to try different machine learning models and approaches, which could improve performance, but a greater benefit is likely to come from using a larger and more heterogeneous set of images to train the model. With a larger dataset ( 𝒪 ⁡ ( 10,000 ) \mathcal{O}(10,000) images) it could also be possible to attempt a multi-class segmentation, enabling the model to distinguish other materials which resemble ivory, such as horns or ivorine, and also to distinguish between various types of ivory. Once the model is optimised, the performances could be further improved using complementary approaches. For example, Ref. [ 10 ] shows promising results using data-mining algorithms to classify the textual information associated with the items offered for sale. Likewise, the recently developed OpenAI’s CLIP framework allows training machine learning classifiers on text and image pair data simultaneously [ 20 ] . Incorporating textual information would increase the robustness of the classification over variations in the way illegal articles are advertised online. Such a multimodal approach would have important practical implications both for law enforcement working in the area of wildlife crime and for the multi-national companies hosting online auction platforms, such as eBay. Currently, the eBay algorithm scans advertisements for the use of “key words” such as “ivory” but it does not have the ability to identify ivory being offered for sale on its platform by the photographs posted by the seller. As previous research has shown, those knowingly offering ivory for sale in contradiction of the laws of the UK and of eBay’s own selling regulations, use pseudonyms to evade text analysis.

The model discussed in this paper, based on photographic image interrogation, could make these kinds of deliberate attempts to circumvent laws and regulations much more difficult. The potential impact of this on conservation is considerable. The use of AI in conservation is growing. Predictive modelling is seen being used in species distribution research and AI-powered technologies, such as sensors are being effectively used in wildlife conservation, monitoring and in anti-poaching efforts [ 17 ] . Technological advancements have been shown to be a useful addition to the intelligence gathering tools used in ‘smart’ law enforcement [ 19 ] and it is both rational and pragmatic to foresee a use for the type of model examined in this paper in wildlife crime law enforcement. For officers, such a model will have profound time-saving implications when investigating ivory being sold through online marketplaces and social media site. However, in addition to the clear law enforcement applications, for online marketplaces and social media sites themselves, such a tool empowers them to control what is advertised for sale on their sites.
